p1.summary: Sets the scene: Farrar, Holmes and the WHO's early-January struggle to pry the virus sequence and reliable epidemiological data out of China.
Zhang's team sequences the new virus from a patient sample on 5 Jan, with Eddie Holmes brought in from Sydney to help analyse it.

China sits on the sequence for weeks despite WHO pressure, until Holmes and Zhang threaten a unilateral release; Farrar and the WHO's Van Kerkhove help force the issue, and Rambaut publishes it on virological.org on 11 Jan.
Tedros publicly thanks China for sharing the sequence ‘in a timely manner’ — rhetoric that papers over the WHO's actual struggle to extract it.
Sets up the WHO's next struggle: getting China to acknowledge human-to-human transmission amid a near-total data blackout.
With the sequence out, the WHO's new problem is the complete absence of any newly reported case for the first two weeks of January.
Farrar directs emerging origin concerns toward the WHO rather than handling them himself.
An under-the-radar first WHO mission to Wuhan on 20–21 Jan turns out to be the WHO's best on-the-ground access for the entire following year.
As Wuhan locks down and China admits human-to-human transmission, a WHO Geneva meeting on 22–23 Jan fails to agree on declaring a PHEIC.
The WHO again declines to declare a PHEIC after Beijing signals it would read one as a vote of no confidence.
The GPMB (with Farrar and Fauci as board members) circulates a draft statement still praising China's ‘transparency’ and ‘collaboration’, even as WHO staff privately fume over stonewalling.

Tedros travels to Beijing and lavishes praise on Xi Jinping's leadership in exchange for only a vague promise of future access — China's own reporting makes clear no return to Wuhan was actually agreed.
Back in Geneva, Tedros piles on more praise for China, enough that the US ambassador privately warns him he is risking his own and the WHO's reputation.
WHO's Michael Ryan loops in Fauci, Farrar and Redfield for an informal chat with Tedros; Farrar separately asks Fauci for his personal views on the virus's origin.
Tedros finally declares a PHEIC on 30 Jan, but frames it explicitly as ‘not a vote of no confidence in China’ and again praises its transparency.
Sets up the thread of early, non-public doubts about the genome's origin reaching Farrar via intelligence channels.

The first press mentions of a possible lab origin (Daily Mail, Washington Times, Washington Post) appear and are quickly dismissed; Sen. Cotton raises the question politically, while Trump keeps praising China for trade reasons.

Baric later testifies he laid out three possible origins — natural, lab escape of a natural virus, or lab escape of an engineered one — at a classified BSEG meeting, though newly released documents suggest the actual date was 29 Jan.

Farrar learns, via unnamed ‘credible scientists’ in the US, that the virus looks ‘almost engineered to infect human cells’ — most likely relayed through his MI5 contacts rather than directly from the scientists themselves.
Farrar consults former MI5 chief Eliza Manningham-Buller and requests a burner phone the same day — Andersen later says he believes the original rumours came from UK intelligence.
On his new burner phone, Farrar asks Holmes to check whether the virus could be a lab escape; Holmes looks at the data and sees nothing suspicious.
Farrar and UK chief scientific adviser Vallance hold a short call with Fauci whose purpose is unclear — Fauci later says under oath he has no memory of it.
Andersen is separately asked to examine the genome, unaware yet of Holmes's own look days earlier.

Andersen calls Holmes and flags three red flags in the genome: a near-perfect RBD, a furin cleavage site in a key spot, and the fact that the WIV had been doing exactly this kind of spike/RBD manipulation.
Holmes tells Andersen he needs to check with his ‘handler’ before going further — Andersen later testifies this confirms Farrar was operating under instruction from UK intelligence.
Farrar briefs Fauci on Andersen's concerns and sends him profiles of Andersen, Garry and Holmes as the scientists involved, asking Fauci to call Andersen directly.
Andersen walks Fauci through the furin cleavage site, the RBD and other oddities; Fauci suggests going public with a paper, but Andersen says it's too early and more analysis is needed.
Fauci proposes widening the review to a larger group of scientists (the future ‘Tony Call’ group) and warns that if Andersen's concerns hold up, the FBI and MI5 would need to be alerted.

Farrar splits the review into an ‘inner group’ (Holmes, Andersen, Garry, Rambaut — the eventual co-authors) and a separate ‘bounce-off’ group (Fouchier, Drosten, Koopmans, Farzan) to satisfy Fauci's request while keeping the core discussion tight; Baric and Daszak are deliberately excluded for having co-published with the WIV.
Fauci forwards a Science article on the genome's clues to Farrar and Andersen; the piece also carries Daszak's public dismissal of Ebright's lab-origin conjecture.
Sets up the first full expert review call that Farrar convenes on 1 Feb to assess Andersen's concerns.
NIH staff scramble from 23 Jan to brief Fauci on NIH-funded EcoHealth Alliance/WIV work, flagging Daszak's R01 grant with Baric as a collaborator.
Just after midnight, Fauci tells his deputy Auchincloss to drop everything and check the scope of NIH's funding relationship with China — Fauci later says this was the first he'd heard of it.

Farrar formally invites the ‘core’ and ‘bounce-off’ groups to a 2pm call; later testimony confirms Tabak and Collins also joined, while whether Baric was quietly on the line at all remains unresolved.
Auchincloss reports back that Daszak's grant never needed the extra P3CO review for risky pathogen work — raising the separate question of whether that oversight framework was actually functioning.
Andersen creates the ‘project-wuhan_engineering’ Slack channel ahead of the call; Holmes previews that the lab-escape idea came from unnamed ‘others’ that Farrar had asked him to look into.

Farrar circulates Rambaut/Andersen/Holmes's sequence-comparison slides, built around six Baric papers on exactly this kind of spike/RBD engineering — with Baric himself excluded from the call over his WIV ties.

The call turns into open conflict: Fouchier and Drosten dismiss any engineering discussion outright, leaving the group unable to agree and concluding the question needs a broader, more formal international process.
Fauci, backed by Collins, suggests the core group write up their doubts as a peer-reviewed paper — premature at this stage, though a confidential report instead would make sense.
Andersen, Holmes and Rambaut hold their own private follow-up call, after which Andersen shares the first draft summary of their analysis on Slack.
Farrar, Fauci, Collins, Vallance and Ferguson hold a short closed-door call of their own to agree next steps — Fauci later says he has no memory of it either.
Farrar writes up a plan to hand the origin question to the WHO using carefully neutral wording, with no mention of Fauci's earlier suggestion to publish a paper.
Fauci briefs a group of HHS officials on the call's outcome, repeating Farrar's neutral framing (typo and all) and noting Farrar and Collins will approach Tedros the next day.
An HHS email shows Fauci's contacts had already been discussing routing the origin question to the WHO before the Farrar call even happened.
Per Spike, the US, UK and Australian intelligence services are briefed on Andersen's findings after the call — Vallance, Holmes and Collins each updating their own country's services.
Sets up the core group's post-call exchange of probability estimates for a lab-related origin.
Despite Fouchier and Drosten's pushback, Farzan and Garry's updated estimates (Farzan: 60:40 to 70:30 for a lab accident) show passaging remains a live hypothesis.
Fouchier argues the question shouldn't go beyond the closed group at all unless a non-natural origin can be shown ‘beyond reasonable doubt’, warning it would otherwise harm science and China.
Farrar pushes back, arguing it's better to address the question openly now than let it fester and polarise later.
Rambaut also pushes back on Fouchier, arguing a non-natural origin could complicate containment and so needs urgent evaluation, not avoidance.
Farrar effectively closes the internal debate, telling the group discussions should pause until the question moves to the WHO — without revealing that HHS had already settled on that plan.

On Slack, Andersen and Rambaut privately dismiss Fouchier and Drosten as ‘too conflicted to think about this issue straight’, agree to route around them going forward, and settle on writing the eventual report ‘erring on the side of extreme caution’ toward a natural-origin conclusion.
Sets up Farrar's follow-up push to Fauci and Collins, introducing passaging as the more realistic non-natural hypothesis after the call's clash.
Collins tells Farrar he's leaning toward a natural origin, echoing some of Fouchier's and Drosten's call-room arguments.

Farrar reintroduces passaging (which Fouchier and Drosten hadn't actually addressed) and makes a prescient call: he's honestly at 50:50, and it will likely ‘remain grey’ unless there's access to the Wuhan lab.
Collins notes the passaging possibility and suggests Wellcome itself could pick up the question if the WHO is too slow; Fauci confirms waiting is not acceptable.
Sets up the parallel diplomatic push to get the WHO to formally take over the origin question.
Farrar struggles to reach Tedros or his chief of staff Schwartländer — a former WHO China representative — to get the broader WHO process moving.

Farrar, Schwartländer and Ryan agree to ask Tedros to take over a forensic investigation of the origin — the email explicitly frames this as getting ‘ahead of the science and the narrative’, which Fauci and Collins also worry the WHO will be too slow to deliver on.
Farrar calls former Chinese health minister Chen Zhu as a back-channel, to warn Beijing that an origin inquiry is coming and to keep communication open regardless of the outcome.
HHS's Grigsby forwards the ‘Tedros Proposal’ document to the WHO's US liaison office, with State Department officials copied in.
Sets up a parallel US ‘Track II’ diplomatic channel, run through the National Academies (NASEM) and China's CAS, to get isolates and data out of China.
Introduces NASEM's Track II science-diplomacy channel with China's CAS (led by LeDuc and Franz), already in use before the outbreak and which would shape the choices made around the Farrar call.

LeDuc flatters Chinese counterparts in a published Op-Ed while quietly asking for virus isolates; NASEM leadership formally backs the request, and by early February CAS's president signals the WIV is willing to share.

A White House-backed request to NASEM for data/isolates turns, at a 3 Feb expert meeting including Andersen, Daszak, Fauci and Baric, into a drafting fight over origin wording — Andersen reports Baric attacking him on the call as pushing ‘crackpot theories’ — ending with the final NASEM letter dodging the origin question entirely.

An ABC article misrepresents the NASEM exercise and quotes Fauci sounding confident the US could tell if the virus were lab-made — alarming China just as Chen Zhu's back-channel outreach was underway, and later fuelling Daszak's resentment of Andersen.

LeDuc tells NASEM's Hamburg an accidental release from the WIV's BSL-3 (though not its BSL-4) work is plausible, then hours later tells intelligence contacts an accidental release is ‘highly unlikely’.
The same day, LeDuc presses the WIV's Yuan Zhiming to ‘fess up’ to any biosafety shortcomings — again at odds with what he'd just told US intelligence about the risk being low.
The OSTP/NASEM effort ends in fiasco: the public misreads it as an origin investigation, and China draws the opposite conclusion from Fauci's comments to the real ask for isolates.
China tells NASEM that isolate-sharing must now go through a WHO framework — leaving the US Track II effort, in LeDuc's own words, unimpressed by the WHO's ability to deliver.
Turns to the drafting of the confidential report that would eventually become the published ‘Proximal Origin’ paper.

Andersen's first one-page draft (1 Feb) flags the BamHI site and the furin cleavage site as the two potentially problematic features, discarding direct gene editing in favour of tissue-culture passage as the leading non-natural hypothesis.
Garry joins the drafting Slack and Google Doc.
Andersen reiterates that accidental escape is ‘highly likely’, not a fringe theory, even as the group narrows who gets to take part in the drafting.
Sets up the moment the draft report is first shared outside the core group, with Fauci and Collins.

Andersen and Holmes finish a four-page draft ruling out deliberate engineering but leaving passaging open; Holmes shares it with Farrar (and from there Fauci and Collins) before Garry — asleep in the US — has even seen it.

Garry finally reviews the draft and flags likely pushback on passaging; the co-authors privately agree a non-natural origin is plausible but decide to ‘give the benefit of the doubt’ to nature in the writing, for political rather than scientific reasons.
Farrar reiterates that the furin cleavage site could be explained by passaging and flags undisclosed Fouchier lab data on forced FCS evolution.

New pangolin sequence data reaches Holmes via a contact already drafting a separate pangolin paper; the co-authors conclude these pangolin viruses are too distant to be SARS-CoV-2's direct progenitor.

The co-authors push to get hold of Farzan's and Fouchier's alluded-to lab data showing passaging can produce a furin site in a coronavirus — data that, tellingly, never surfaces in any P.O. draft or the final paper.
The WHO formally agrees to take up the origin question.
Farrar gets the WHO's go-ahead to convene an origins-and-evolution group at its meeting the following week.
Both Koopmans and the WHO independently float publishing the report directly, as a way to pre-empt conspiracy theories.
Farrar asks the co-authors, via Holmes, whether they should publish the report rather than keep it confidential.
Farrar also asks for the ‘conspiracy’ language in the draft to be dampened down and made ‘totally neutral’.

On Slack, Garry, Rambaut and Andersen agree passaging remains genuinely plausible but worry publishing could be career-ending and hand the WHO a political problem; Rambaut recalls how badly a past scientist was pilloried for suggesting a lab escape.
Covers the day a (false) pangolin-virus homology claim and Farrar's decision to publish collide.

A Chinese university (SCAU) announces pangolin coronaviruses ‘99% similar’ to SARS-CoV-2 — later shown to be false — triggering what Holmes calls ‘pangomania’; Koopmans publicly urges caution before the sequences are even published.
The draft's ‘Evolution of 2019-nCoV’ section is quietly renamed ‘Origin of 2019-nCoV’ — a wording shift the piece argues is misleading, since the content never actually addresses outbreak origin.
Farrar flags the SCAU pangolin claim to Fauci and Collins as potentially the ‘missing link’; Collins immediately asks the key question — does it have the furin cleavage site?

Farrar decides to go for publication and starts planning author list, journals (Lancet, Nature, NEJM) and WHO sign-off with Holmes — a decision the piece argues both had their own separate reasons to want, independent of the still-unverified pangolin news.
Holmes shares Farrar's publication decision with the co-drafters, who push to see the actual SCAU pangolin sequence (and whether it has a furin site) before going any further.
The full ‘Tony Call’ group sees the draft and the publication plan for the first time, and some of them push back.
Farrar sends the draft to the wider call group (Fouchier, Koopmans, Drosten, Vallance, Ferguson, Golding) for the first time, asking whether it should be published.

Fouchier argues passaging should also be rejected, on the (weak) grounds that nobody is known to have worked on a close viral relative in China — an argument the piece says later shapes his and Daszak's move to torpedo the manuscript at Nature.
Ferguson's feedback says the glycan shield isn't incompatible with passaging, and confirms Tabak (a glycoprotein expert) was on the original Farrar call.
Vallance backs publication, leaning against passaging and wanting the glycans used as further evidence for a natural origin.
Garry and Rambaut float offering SCAU a Nature co-publication (even the cover) in exchange for early access to their pangolin sequence.
The group debates whether the spike protein's glycan shield rules out passaging; Garry and Rambaut conclude it doesn't — the same immune-driven signature would appear either way.

Drosten, largely absent since the original call, asks bluntly whether they're ‘debunking our own conspiracy theory’ — seemingly unaware the group had already shifted from engineering to the still-live passaging question.

Holmes explains the point was always to also address a credible accidental-escape scenario, not just outlandish bioweapon claims — while the piece notes the group's key counter-argument (no known close relative in Chinese labs) rests on knowledge nobody actually had.

Holmes, Farrar and (more hesitantly) Rambaut all say the pangolin data now has them leaning toward a natural origin and support publishing — reasoning the piece calls backwards, arguments assembled to fit a conclusion already reached.
Privately on Slack, Andersen dismisses Fouchier's ‘no lab has passaged a close relative’ argument by noting exactly that kind of work was being done in Wuhan, in BSL-2.
Andersen alone pushes back on publishing now, saying it's premature without seeing the actual pangolin data first.
Farrar firmly overrules Andersen's objection and makes clear he wants a ‘conclusive’ statement that becomes ‘the go-to scientific statement to refer to’ — and the co-authors fall in line.
Fouchier shifts his argument again, inadvertently conceding — as Andersen notes — that the sequence data alone can't actually rule out deliberate engineering either.

Holmes admits the ‘99%’ pangolin homology was actually ‘up to 99%’ and overstated — news that never reaches the wider call group or visibly changes the drafts, even as Farrar pushes ahead toward publication regardless.

p2.summary: Sets up the converging pressure from NASEM, the US government and the WHO, all independently racing to get access to China in the second week of February.
Farrar reaches out to NASEM president Victor Dzau to share his analysis of the virus's origins — the first time he mentions his effort to Dzau at all.
Farrar tweets publicly demanding new SARS-CoV-2 sequences from Wuhan, noting none had been published since 4 Jan.

Tedros declares the WHO is ‘battling the trolls and conspiracy theorists’ — unusually combative rhetoric that, the piece argues, was really about shoring up his negotiating position with China just as the WHO needed access.
Farrar and Holmes brief Dzau's NASEM team by phone, with Andersen privately doubtful the initiative will amount to much — not yet aware that the hyped pangolin sequence was about to disappoint.
China's ambassador calls Sen. Tom Cotton's lab-escape questions ‘absolutely crazy’ on US television, while deflecting on whether CDC experts will actually be let into China.
After ten days of negotiation, a three-person WHO advance team finally departs for Beijing to negotiate terms for a larger mission — a mission the piece notes nobody even noticed.

Tedros's vague hope that the WHO team might include US CDC experts alarms Washington; the WHO's own right-hand man bluntly tells the US it is just one country among many, despite being its largest funder.
Sets up the mounting pressure Farrar comes under to actually deliver the publication he has promised.

The long-awaited ‘environmental’ market samples turn out to be genetically identical to early patient sequences — spectacularly uninformative, as Holmes puts it — deepening doubts that the market was really the source, while Drosten separately tells Rambaut he thinks the virus had already been circulating in humans for a while.
Koopmans, unaware the pangolin match had already been downgraded, argues any lab-escape scenario should be buried in the discussion section rather than addressed head-on in the paper's body.

Farrar politely but firmly tells Fouchier, Koopmans and Drosten that his decision is final and the co-authors will take it from there — a decision the piece argues had nothing to do with the WHO being ‘too busy’, as Farrar later claimed, and everything to do with Fauci's own remarks days earlier that the US could determine if the virus was lab-made.

Fauci sits in for only five or ten minutes of a meeting on regulatory compliance for Baric's 2015 chimera paper before excusing himself for a secure call — an exit Baric himself found a little odd, and which the piece reads as deliberate deniability.
Covers the week the co-authors spend finishing the manuscript for publication.

Ian Lipkin, flagging that ‘higher-ups’ and intelligence contacts share his concern about the furin cleavage site, is recruited as a co-author partly to help counterbalance the Fouchier-Koopmans-Drosten opposition.
Within 36 hours, Andersen pitches Nature's senior editor, Farrar calls the editor-in-chief directly, and Holmes closes the loop — Nature agrees to consider the piece.
The co-authors sketch extra explanatory figures, including one joking use of Daszak's own photo to illustrate the ‘lab passage’ scenario — none of which makes the final draft.
With Andersen on a break, Holmes — most fluent in the pangolin sequences and most in tune with Farrar — takes over editing the manuscript.

Just as Nature shows interest, the passaging section is quietly downgraded from a live hypothesis to ‘extremely unlikely’ with no discussion on Slack explaining why — a change Andersen may not even have seen before leaving on his break.
Sets up how a hostile domestic press cycle around Tom Cotton collided with the WHO's delicate mission into China.
The full WHO team begins its first day of meetings in Beijing with no visit to Wuhan yet agreed, and no clarity on what access China is actually willing to give.
US ambassador Andrew Bremberg presses Tedros directly for Wuhan access just as the full mission arrives.

The Washington Post savages Tom Cotton's Fox News remarks on a possible lab escape as a ‘conspiracy theory... repeatedly debunked’, even though Cotton had explicitly said there was no evidence either way.
US media largely falls in behind the Washington Post's framing, hardening the question of the virus's origin into a partisan one almost overnight.
Covers the frantic 48 hours in which the manuscript goes from draft to public release.
The co-authors, minus Andersen (on vacation), finalise author order and reviewers; Holmes stresses the piece presents no new data of its own, and the group expects a fast, easy peer review.
Garry circulates the Washington Post's attack on Cotton as fresh justification for getting the manuscript out quickly.
Collins urges publication ‘ASAP’; Lipkin reports both Farrar and Collins ‘very happy’ — the priority now is getting Nature's blessing to post a preprint while formal review continues.
Acting on ‘pressure from on high’, Holmes submits the manuscript to Nature at 2:30 am UK — hours before Andersen, officially due to send it himself, is even back from his break.
Nature's editor green-lights releasing the manuscript publicly while formal peer review is still underway.
Rambaut formats and uploads the final text to his own virological.org board — which Daszak's Statement of Support in Lancet would cite within hours.
Farrar asks to be sent the finished text immediately so the WHO can see it ‘ASAP’ — Garry notes on Slack it ‘makes a much stronger case against bioengineering’.
Andersen privately concedes ‘the guy isn't totally wrong’ about Cotton, while Farrar confirms to Lipkin that the Cotton controversy is part of why he wants rapid publication.

Farrar asks for ‘unlikely’ to become ‘improbable’ on deliberate engineering — a change Andersen considers trivial, since passaging, not engineering, is what the co-authors actually still consider live.

Farrar asks the co-authors to take the manuscript down from virological.org so he can instead stage a press conference — evidence, the piece argues, that Farrar saw himself as effectively owning the paper he had commissioned.
Andersen refuses to remove the manuscript or hold it for a press release, wary that moving it to a formal preprint server would make it look institutionally sanctioned.
Farrar presses for a release date so he can coordinate press briefings to ensure ‘the key messages are reasonably reported’.
Andersen tells Farrar that bioRxiv doesn't accept opinion pieces — a technicality that conveniently sidesteps airing his deeper doubts about the manuscript's readiness.
Farrar retweets Andersen's thread, tagging the WHO's top officials directly.
NIAID staff check in on the manuscript's progress toward peer-reviewed publication, confirming the NIH's own strong interest in seeing it formally published.
Turns to Daszak's parallel effort to pre-empt the origin question with his own public statement.

Daszak begins drafting his ‘Statement of Support’ explicitly to close gaps he sees in the NASEM letter — not realising the reassuring language he's relying on had already been struck from the final version.
After Baric declines to sign over conflict-of-interest concerns, Daszak decides not to sign either — then signs anyway while still concealing that he wrote and organised the whole thing.
Daszak folds Tedros's ‘trolls and conspiracy theorists’ line straight into his draft, later softened for the final published version.
The co-authors read Daszak's letter as a pre-emptive strike against the passaging hypothesis, mocking him as the ‘Grand wizard of EgoHealth’ leading the ‘Ego krewe’.
What started as an online petition becomes, thanks to Farrar's direct intervention with Lancet's editor, a publication in one of the world's most prestigious medical journals within two days.

Daszak complains that ‘conspiracy theories’ have reached high levels of the US government — effectively confirming that the unresolved NASEM letter had let the origin question travel further than he wanted.
Daszak's Statement is published simultaneously on change.org and in Lancet, with Baric and Linfa Wang conspicuously absent from the signatory list.
Farrar tweets about Daszak's Statement; Daszak, trying to keep his authorship quiet, replies in a way deliberately readable as either a general thank-you or an acknowledgment of his hidden role.
Covers the week in which the pangolin evidence the co-authors were counting on falls apart.
A fresh GISAID upload briefly raises hopes before Holmes clarifies it's just his own, unrelated pangolin preprint — with no furin cleavage site at all.
The actual SCAU sequences finally appear: no furin site, and the hyped ‘up to 99%’ similarity turns out to average just 90.3% — Holmes admits SCAU ‘totally over-hyped in the press release’.
Both pangolin preprints confirm the viruses are too distant to be SARS-CoV-2's direct progenitor, leaving the origin question wide open again despite the SCAU press conference's early claims.
With the pangolin lead dead, Andersen starts treating passaging as a ‘quite a high probability’ explanation for the RBD — just two days after the manuscript downplayed it in stealth mode.
Covers Nature's rejection of the manuscript and the scramble that follows.
Nature turns the manuscript down: Reviewer #2 warns it could fuel conspiracy theories by even mentioning lab-escape, and Nature itself worries the piece will quickly go out of date.
Andersen fires back within an hour, insisting a lab origin ‘must be considered a serious scientific theory... not dismissed out of hand as another conspiracy theory’.
Holmes and Garry conclude Reviewer #2 thinks exactly like Fouchier, and suspect the reviewer sent Nature's editor an alarming private note behind the scenes.
The co-authors agree to draft a rebuttal and ask Farrar to lean on Nature's editor-in-chief directly, while preparing a fallback submission to Nature Medicine.
Covers the discovery of a new bat virus, RmYN02, and how it reshapes — and ultimately kills — the passaging argument.
Holmes hears early ‘rumblings’ of a bat virus with a furin cleavage site — information that, Andersen and Garry note, wouldn't actually rule out any of their three scenarios.

Nature itself publishes an editor's note favouring a market origin, and a TWiV podcast episode turns the manuscript's deliberate ambiguity into a one-sided case against any lab escape — pressure the co-authors increasingly feel from ‘reliable’ scientific sources.
Holmes privately shares the still-unpublished RmYN02 bat sequence, revealing he has quietly joined its authoring team over the preceding weekend.

RmYN02 shows that furin-site-like insertions are possible in nature — a fact the co-authors stretch, the piece argues, from evidence that passaging isn't necessary into justification for dropping it as implausible.
The co-authors reach for weak, shifting arguments to avoid even mentioning the possibility of a researcher being infected by a natural virus handled in a lab.

The co-authors agree to rush out the RmYN02 paper, rewrite the manuscript to further downgrade the lab-product hypothesis, and switch to the WHO's preferred name, HCoV-19, over the official SARS-CoV-2.
The final stretch to publication, this time in Nature Medicine.
Holmes threatens to pull his name from the paper rather than let it specify which part of the genome came from where, forcing the co-authors to stay vague about the RBD's actual origin.
With the publication window closing, the co-authors pivot to Nature Medicine and decide to reference RmYN02 only obliquely, so as to ‘look wicked smart’ once the real paper comes out.
Nature Medicine agrees to reuse Nature's existing peer review, and after some final cuts and edits, the manuscript is formally transferred and accepted within a week.
Andersen thanks Farrar, Fauci and Collins for their ‘advice and leadership’ as the manuscript clears its final hurdle.

Hours before publication, Daszak emails Baric that he's confident the White House's new OSTP committee won't revisit the origin question — a prognosis the piece notes was ‘way off’, since the Lijian Zhao wolf-warrior flare-up hits that very same day.

Proximal Origin is published, with Nature's own tweet calling it a ‘paper’ that shows the virus is ‘not a laboratory construct’ — the same day Trump's ‘Chinese virus’ comment ignites a controversy that, the piece notes, became the paper's accidental marketing.
NIAID is formally notified of the publication, closing the loop on the update request from three weeks earlier.

Scripps' press release headline (‘natural origin... scientists say’) overstates what Andersen's own words actually claimed, quietly erasing the lab-escape-of-a-natural-virus scenario the paper never addressed.
Sets up the geopolitical backdrop — Trump's shift from praising China to the ‘Chinese virus’ controversy — against which Proximal Origin lands.
Through early March, Trump stays conciliatory toward China while chasing a trade deal, criticised at the time only for downplaying the pandemic's risk — not for blaming China for it.

As the trade deal fades and tensions rise, Pompeo calls it ‘incredibly frustrating’ to get data from China and uses the term ‘Wuhan virus’ on 6 Mar — a complaint the piece judges factually correct, if not widely recognised as such at the time.
China's Foreign Ministry spokesman Zhao Lijian goes on the offensive, suggesting the US army brought the virus to Wuhan; the Chinese ambassador is summoned to the State Department the next day.
On the evening of 16 Mar, Trump tweets about the ‘Chinese virus’ for the first time, explaining it as a response to China's own false claim that the US military had brought the virus there.
China reacts angrily and expels NYT, WSJ and Washington Post journalists on 17 Mar, the same day US media frame Trump's tweet as straightforward racism — and P.O. is published.
Compares the published Nature Medicine text against the earlier virological.org draft, line by line.
Key phrasing shifts from ‘genetic engineering’ to ‘purposeful manipulation’, and from ‘necessary’ to ‘plausible’ — changes that, the piece argues, quietly widen what the paper claims to rule out.

The paper's single most-cited sentence is shown to be logically vacuous: finding ‘all notable features’ in nature elsewhere is equally consistent with either a natural origin or a lab-engineered one built from those same natural parts.

The paper's ‘parsimony’ claim for a natural RBD is exposed as comparing the wrong kind of odds — generic background probability instead of the actual circumstances (timing, location, known research) of the outbreak.
Covers the co-authors' own private second-guessing in the weeks after publication, as doubts about Proximal Origin's conclusions start resurfacing.
The paper becomes a runaway success — three million views within a month — and the co-authors spend weeks simply enjoying its Altmetric score.
A Washington Post opinion piece reveals State Department cables taking a lab leak seriously — this time coming from inside the administration, not dismissed as Cotton-style conspiracy.
Collins frets that Proximal Origin hasn't killed the ‘destructive conspiracy’; Fauci dismisses it as ‘a shiny object that will go away in time’.

Fauci cites Proximal Origin from the White House podium to rebut a reporter's lab-origin question — a paper, the piece notes, that had itself been written specifically to appease China and smooth the WHO's access, with Fauci's own earlier remarks part of what made that appeasement necessary.
Privately, Andersen admits he still can't rule out engineering or passaging, undercutting the very confidence Fauci had just projected publicly.
Holmes offers a string of weak counter-arguments against Andersen's doubts; Andersen politely but firmly holds his ground on BSL-2 culturing work at the WIV as a genuine concern.
The co-authors return to celebrating the paper's renewed Altmetric score, even as Andersen takes an unexpectedly political stance on a White House advisory call.

A reflective recap: the co-authors, cornered between the WHO's need for access and the NIH's preferred narrative, quietly set a much higher bar of proof for a lab origin than for a natural one — the asymmetry the piece says explains the whole drafting process.
Covers an anonymous 2020 attempt to discredit the Proximal Origin authors, and the piece's own speculation about who sent it.

An anonymous email to journalist Jon Cohen accuses the Proximal Origin authors of having needed to be ‘schooled’ by real experts on the Farrar call, and claims Nature initially rejected the paper over this.
Rather than publish it, Cohen forwards the email straight to Andersen and Holmes, who — with Farrar, Fauci and Wellcome's own comms team — draft and send a rebuttal within 24 hours.
The email's own wording points to someone who was on the original Farrar call — most likely Fouchier or Koopmans.
The piece narrows the likely motive to either genuine authorship grievance, or a deliberate attempt to damage the authors' reputations.
Despite Holmes's suspicion, the piece argues Baric is an implausible suspect — he had nothing to gain and would go on to publicly call for a proper origins investigation.
The piece argues an authorship motive doesn't hold up either, since neither Fouchier nor Drosten — the ones who actually shaped the paper's conclusions — ever showed interest in claiming credit.
The email's odd fixation on what Fauci ‘first’ believed, rather than the authorship question it claims to raise, is read as a tell about who really wrote it.
The email's date and opening line tie it directly to a Science article published the day before, quoting Daszak, Holmes and Andersen together.
The email's careful effort to exempt Lipkin from blame points toward someone protective of him — and of his long-standing ties to the Global Virome Project.

Pulling the clues together, the piece builds a profile and a motive — protecting Daszak's Global Virome Project and NIH funding from Andersen, Holmes and Rambaut — without ever naming a suspect outright.
Steps back to the years-long feud and funding rivalry between Daszak and the Proximal Origin authors that the piece argues shaped much of this story.
Traces years of public sniping between Daszak's Global Virome Project and Holmes/Andersen/Rambaut's rival surveillance approach, through journal comments, rebuttals and conference jabs.
Andersen publicly mocks Daszak's PREDICT funding complaints as ‘hyped marketing claims’, directly threatening the funding model Daszak's whole operation depends on.
Andersen and Rambaut publicly call out EcoHealth Alliance for publishing the new coronavirus's sequence tree without crediting Zhang and Holmes, who actually did the work.

Daszak complains to a colleague that the Proximal Origin authors are ‘the exact same group’ who pushed the lab-leak question all the way to the White House — the very scientists he blames for jeopardising his own grants.

After the NIH suspends his R01 grant following Proximal Origin's publication, Daszak — backed quietly by Fauci's advisor Morens — spends months fighting to reverse it, blaming political interference even as his funding model (PREDICT, the GVP) keeps unravelling.
